title: Mother's Face at the Visual Cliff
text:
The visual cliff is a sheet of strong glass laid over a checkered surface. On one side the pattern sits right under the glass; on the other it drops away, so that it looks as if the floor ends in a sudden fall. In the 1980s, James Sorce, Robert Emde, Joseph Campos and Mary Klinnert at the University of Denver used a version with a modest drop to ask how babies decide what to do when a situation is unclear.

One-year-olds were placed on the shallow side, with an attractive toy beyond the apparent drop and their mother standing on the far side. The drop was set at a height that made babies hesitate rather than refuse outright. As they reached the edge, most looked up at their mother's face.

The mothers had been trained to show a particular expression. When the mother looked happy, most of the babies crossed the glass to her. When she showed fear, none of them crossed. Other expressions, such as interest or anger, produced results in between.

The study became a classic demonstration of social referencing: when infants are uncertain, they look to a trusted adult and use that adult's emotion to decide whether to go ahead.
lesson: Children read your face to learn what is safe and what is dangerous. Your calm or your fear becomes theirs, so notice what you are showing them.
people: James Sorce, Robert Emde, Joseph Campos, Mary Klinnert
source: Sorce, J. F., Emde, R. N., Campos, J., and Klinnert, M. D. (1985). Maternal emotional signaling: Its effect on the visual cliff behavior of 1-year-olds. Developmental Psychology, 21(1), 195-200.
